Tobar Segais An ordinary salmon ate nine hazelnuts that fell into Tobar Segais - the Well
of Wisdom - from the nine hazel trees that surrounded the well, and gained
all the world's knowledge. — Irish mythology Tobar Segais serves versioned documentation archives. Point it at a directory
of .zip or .jar files and it publishes each one at a stable URL, with a
navigation tree, full-text search and a version picker. It is a single static binary. There is no application server, no JVM and no
database. This site is the demo Everything here is served by Tobar Segais, and every manual in the sidebar is
an archive in a directory: The user manual — how to publish
documentation to it and how to run it. The version picker on it reaches the
1.15 and 1.16 manuals, which are the original Eclipse InfoCenter bundles from
the 1.x releases, served unchanged. Bundles from Markdown , from AsciiDoc and from Typst — one manual for each source
format, each documenting how to publish that format, and each published that
way. Get it $ go install github.com/tobar-segais/tobar-segais/cmd/tobar-segais@latest Or run the image: $ docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/content:/content" \
    ghcr.io/tobar-segais/tobar-segais:latest Binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows are attached to each release . Elsewhere The source Follow @tobarsegais

About this site This site is built by the tool it documents. Nothing here is hand-written HTML. How it is made Every push to main runs a workflow that: builds an archive from each directory of source — docs/ for the user
manual, and one for each of the format manuals — with tobar-segais bundle ; copies in the 1.15 and 1.16 archives, which are the original Eclipse
InfoCenter bundles from the 1.x releases and are served exactly as they
were published; generates the whole site from that directory with tobar-segais build ,
which writes every page, the assets and a search index; publishes the result. So the site is a static snapshot with no server behind it, and the same
templates render it as would render it live. What you can do here that a
served site could also do — navigate, search, switch versions — is doing it
without a server; what you cannot do is add an archive and watch it appear,
which is the one thing publishing gives up. See Static sites in the manual. The name Tobar Segais is the well the river of knowledge rises from, and the salmon of
knowledge swims in that river. The current in the banner above runs right to
left, because the salmon at the source is swimming into it.

Introduction This manual documents how to publish AsciiDoc documentation to Tobar Segais.
It is itself written in AsciiDoc and published that way, as is the server’s own
user manual. What the server needs A bundle is a zip containing HTML pages and a navigation document. Asciidoctor produces both. What you need installed Asciidoctor, on PATH . Either implementation will do: the Ruby one, or asciidoctor.js from npm.
They take the same flags and produce the same output. The server invokes it for you: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content Detection is by file extension, so a directory of .adoc files is recognised
as AsciiDoc without being told. If your Asciidoctor is not on PATH under that name — a user gem, or inside bundle exec — point at it: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --tool "bundle exec asciidoctor" Why AsciiDoc It is the format that needs the least glue.
Cross-references rewrite themselves to the generated files, and a docinfo file
carries the bundle’s identity, so nothing has to be restated in a second
format.

The navigation document Every bundle needs a nav.adoc . It carries the tree of pages and, with a docinfo.html beside it, the identity of the bundle. The tree A nested list of cross-references: = The Handbook
:slug: handbook
:revnumber: 1.0.0
:docinfo: shared
:docinfodir: .

* xref:index.adoc[Introduction]
* Guides
** xref:install.adoc[Installing]
** xref:upgrade.adoc[Upgrading] Cross-references point at the .adoc sources , and Asciidoctor rewrites
them to the generated .html files. Unlike Markdown, no textual substitution
is involved: the rewriting is done by the converter, so it is reliable. An entry with no cross-reference, like Guides , becomes a heading that groups
its children without being a page itself. Identity Put a docinfo.html next to nav.adoc : <meta name="tobar-segais.slug" content="{slug}">
<meta name="tobar-segais.version" content="{revnumber}"> Asciidoctor substitutes the attributes and copies this into the generated
head. The document title becomes the bundle title. So the slug, the version, the title and the navigation are all declared once,
in the header of nav.adoc . Neither is required. A bundle with no docinfo.html at all takes its slug and
version from the filename, so handbook-1.0.0.zip is handbook at 1.0.0 .
Declaring them is worth it when the version comes from the build rather than
from whoever names the file. The slug must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens: it goes straight into
a URL. The version is compared using semantic versioning, so 2.0.0-rc1 sorts
below 2.0.0 and is never chosen as the latest.

Building and publishing One command tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content That converts every .adoc page, converts nav.adoc into the navigation
document, and writes a zip named from the slug and version the bundle
declares. What the tool runs Pages are a plain invocation: asciidoctor -o page.html page.adoc Whatever Asciidoctor wraps the content in — the head, the embedded
stylesheet, the footer with its "Last updated" timestamp — is removed
afterwards. The title survives, because in full output it is already an <h1> . The navigation document is converted whole, because its head is the point: asciidoctor -a docinfosubs=attributes -o nav.html nav.adoc Asciidoctor embeds a complete stylesheet in every full document.
The tool strips stylesheets from the generated HTML afterwards, so no flag is
needed to suppress something that would only be discarded. Publishing Write the bundle where the server is watching: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out /srv/docs The server notices within moments. There is nothing to restart. Assets Images and other files next to the sources are copied into the bundle with
their layout intact, so relative references from a page keep working.

Caveats Few, compared with the other formats, but worth knowing. docinfo naming is easy to get wrong :docinfo: shared reads docinfo.html . :docinfo: private reads <docname>-docinfo.html — so for nav.adoc that is nav-docinfo.html . Naming the file docinfo.html while declaring private produces no error and
no meta tags: the file is simply not found, and the bundle falls back to being
identified by its filename. If a bundle appears under an unexpected slug, this
is the first thing to check. Attributes are not substituted unless you ask Docinfo content is copied verbatim by default, so {slug} would reach the
output literally. -a docinfosubs=attributes enables substitution; the tool
passes it. Pages need no flags Asciidoctor is invoked plainly, and its output is cleaned afterwards.
You do not need -s , and you should not use it: in embedded mode the
document title is omitted unless -a showtitle is also given, and the tool
relies on the title being present. The two implementations agree Ruby Asciidoctor and asciidoctor.js accept the same flags and, in this
manual’s case, produce byte-identical pages.
The only difference is the generator meta element in the navigation
document, which names the version that built it and is not used for anything. Section ids are generated for you Asciidoctor gives every section an id, which the server uses to build the On this page column. Nothing extra is required, but if you set :idprefix: or :idseparator: the anchors change accordingly.

Introduction This manual documents how to publish Markdown documentation to Tobar Segais.
It is itself written in Markdown and published that way. What the server needs A bundle is a zip containing HTML pages and a navigation document. What you need installed Nothing. Markdown is rendered inside the tool, so unlike AsciiDoc and Typst there is no
external converter to install: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content Detection is by file extension, so a directory of .md files is recognised as
Markdown without being told. Which Markdown GitHub Flavored Markdown , by way of goldmark — the same renderer Hugo uses.
That means CommonMark, plus tables, strikethrough, task lists and autolinks. Definition lists and footnotes are enabled as well, which GFM itself does not
specify.

The navigation document Every bundle needs a nav.md . It carries the tree of pages, and the identity
of the bundle in its front matter. The tree A nested list of links: - [Introduction](index.md)
- Guides
  - [Installing](install.md)
  - [Upgrading](upgrade.md) Links point at the .md sources , and are rewritten to the generated .html pages during conversion. So the same file works as navigation and as
something you can follow in an editor or on a git host. The rewriting happens on the parsed document rather than by editing text, so a
reference-style link, or one split across lines, is handled correctly. An entry with no link, like Guides , becomes a heading that groups its
children without being a page itself. Identity YAML front matter at the top of nav.md : ---
slug: handbook
version: 1.0.0
title: The Handbook
--- None of it is required. A bundle with no front matter at all takes its slug
and version from the filename, so handbook-1.0.0.zip is handbook at 1.0.0 . title , aliases and hidden are optional too, and mean what they do
everywhere else. The slug must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens: it goes straight into
a URL. The version is compared using semantic versioning, so 2.0.0-rc1 sorts
below 2.0.0 and is never chosen as the latest. Front matter on the other pages is ignored, so you can keep whatever your
editor or git host expects there.

Building and publishing One command tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content That renders every .md page, renders nav.md into the navigation document,
and writes a zip named from the slug and version the front matter declares. What happens Pages are rendered as fragments, because the server supplies the surrounding
page: its own layout, the navigation tree, the version pills and search. The navigation document is rendered as a whole document, because its head is
where the identity goes. Section ids are generated automatically from headings, and the server uses
them to build the On this page column. Publishing Write the bundle where the server is watching: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out /srv/docs The server notices within moments. There is nothing to restart. Assets Images and other files next to the sources are copied into the bundle with
their layout intact, so relative references from a page keep working.

Caveats Markdown is the least troublesome of the three formats, because nothing is
shelled out to. Raw HTML is passed through, then filtered Markdown permits inline HTML, and it survives into the page. The server strips <script> elements and inline event handlers when it renders content, so a
help page cannot run code in the container's origin. Do not rely on scripts in documentation; they will not run. Front matter belongs on the navigation document slug and version are read from nav.md only. Front matter on other pages
is parsed and ignored, which is deliberate: a page cannot rename the bundle
it happens to sit in. Only relative links are rewritten Links to .md files are rewritten to .html . Anything with a scheme is left
exactly as written, so external links are never touched. Nesting is CommonMark's A sub-list is indented to line up with its parent's content — two spaces after
a - marker. This is CommonMark's rule, and it is not what every Markdown
tool does; some require four. If a group's children are missing from the sidebar, check the indentation.

Introduction This manual documents how to publish Typst documentation to Tobar Segais. It is itself written in Typst and published that way, so what you are reading is the output of the process it describes. What the server needs A bundle is a zip containing HTML pages and a navigation document. Typst's HTML export produces both, so no other tooling is involved. Two ways to lay out a manual A page per file One .typ per page, and a nav.typ listing them. This manual is built that way. One source, many documents A single book.typ or main.typ that emits each page with #document , using Typst's bundle export. This suits something written as a book. Both are described in Books and multiple files . The tool chooses between them by looking for a nav.typ . What you need installed Typst, on PATH . The server invokes it for you: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content Detection is by file extension, so a directory of .typ files is recognised as Typst without being told. If your Typst is somewhere unusual, point at it with --tool .

The navigation document Every bundle needs a navigation document. It carries the tree of pages and the identity of the bundle. In a page-per-file layout it is nav.typ . With bundle export it is whatever your source emits as nav.html . The content is the same either way. The tree Write it as a list of links. Nesting becomes nesting: - #link("index.html")[Introduction] - Guides - #link("install.html")[Installing] - #link("upgrade.html")[Upgrading] Links point at the generated .html files, not at the .typ sources. Typst has no cross-reference form that rewrites extensions, so this is one place where Typst is more manual than AsciiDoc. An entry with no link, like Guides , becomes a heading that groups its children without being a page itself. Identity Slug and version are declared as HTML meta elements, and the title as a title element: #html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.slug", content: "handbook")) #html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.version", content: "1.0.0")) #html.elem("title")[The Handbook] Typst emits these into the document body rather than its head. The server reads meta elements wherever they appear, so this works, but it is worth knowing if you inspect the generated file and wonder why the head looks bare. Neither is required. A bundle with no metadata at all takes its slug and version from the filename, so handbook-1.0.0.zip is handbook at 1.0.0 . The slug must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens: it goes straight into a URL. The version is compared using semantic versioning.

Building and publishing One command tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content The tool detects Typst from the file extensions, works out which layout you are using, converts accordingly, and writes a zip named from the slug and version the bundle declares. What the tool runs For a page per file, each page and the navigation document separately: typst compile --format html --features html page.typ page.html For a book, one compilation that writes every file: typst compile --features html,bundle --format bundle book.typ out/ --features html is required because HTML export is not yet enabled by default, and bundle likewise for bundle export. The tool passes them for you. Publishing Write the bundle where the server is watching: tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out /srv/docs The server notices within moments. There is nothing to restart. Assets Images and other files next to the sources are copied into the bundle with their layout intact, so relative references from a page keep working. Files whose names begin with an underscore are treated as partials and are not published.

Books and multiple files Typst joins files with #include , producing one document. A documentation bundle wants a page per file, each with its own address. There are two ways to bridge that, and Typst supports both. Keeping one source Typst's bundle export lets a single compilation write several files, each declared with #document : #document("nav.html")[ #html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.slug", content: "handbook")) #html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.version", content: "1.0.0")) #html.elem("title")[The Handbook] - #link("index.html")[Introduction] - #link("chapter-two.html")[The second chapter] ] #document("index.html")[ = Introduction ... ] Name that file book.typ or main.typ , leave out nav.typ , and the tool uses bundle export: tobar-segais bundle ./book --out ./content detected typst source bundle export from book.typ This suits a book that already exists as one source. Chapters can stay in separate files and be pulled in with #import , while each #document call decides what becomes a page. The navigation document is emitted the same way, so identity and tree still come from the source. A page per file The alternative is one .typ per page and a nav.typ listing them, as this manual uses. The tool picks this when a nav.typ is present. Each page is compiled on its own, so it cannot rely on setup performed by a parent. This fails: = Third chapter #note[A helper defined elsewhere.] with error: unknown variable: note . Import what the page needs: #import "_common.typ": note Partials A file whose name begins with an underscore is a partial: pulled into other files, never a page of its own. Put shared setup in _common.typ and it stays out of the navigation and out of the bundle. The same convention applies to every format. Which to choose Use bundle export for something that is a book: written as one work, read in order, where the chapters share setup. Use a page per file for something that is a manual: pages that are written, reviewed and linked to separately. What replaces the outline #outline() builds a table of contents from headings and links to anchors within one document. In a bundle the server provides that instead: the navigation tree spans pages and versions, and the On this page column is built from each page's own headings.

Caveats Typst's HTML export is young. These are the things that bite. HTML export is experimental Typst prints a warning on every compile saying so, and its authors reserve the right to change the behaviour. Bundle export carries the same warning. Treat Typst bundles as a preview rather than a production commitment. Headings shift down a level, and that is fine The exporter reserves h1 for the document title, so = in source becomes h2 in output, == becomes h3 , and so on. You cannot correct this in Typst: #set heading(offset: -1) fails to compile, because offsets must be zero or more. You do not need to. The server normalises headings when it renders a page, so the shallowest heading on the page becomes h1 and the rest follow. Write = for the page title and == for sections, as you would for a PDF, and the result matches every other format. Lists use a hyphen - starts a list item. * is strong emphasis, so a line beginning with * is read as an unclosed delimiter and fails to compile. This is easy to get wrong coming from Markdown or AsciiDoc. Pages cannot inherit setup In a page-per-file layout each page is compiled on its own, so a helper or a #set rule defined in another file is not in scope. Import what the page needs from a partial. See Books and multiple files . Not every element has an HTML form Layout-oriented features have no meaning in HTML and are either dropped or reported as unsupported. Typst is a typesetting language first; its HTML output is a second target, not the primary one. If a construct does not survive, that is a limitation of the exporter rather than of the bundle format.

An ordinary salmon ate nine hazelnuts that fell into Tobar Segais - the Well of
Wisdom - from the nine hazel trees that surrounded the well, and gained all the
world’s knowledge. — Irish mythology Introduction Tobar Segais serves versioned documentation archives.
Point it at a directory of .zip or .jar files and it publishes each one at
a stable URL, with a navigation tree, full-text search and a version picker. It is a single static binary with no runtime dependencies.
There is no application server, no JVM and no database. It does not have to run at all. The same content can be written out as a
static site — pages, assets and a search index that is queried in the browser — and hosted on GitHub Pages or anything else that serves files. See Static sites . What changed in 2.0 Version 2.0 is a rewrite in Go.
The 1.x releases were a Java web application that ran in a servlet container
and read its content from inside its own WAR file. The differences that matter day to day: Content is no longer packaged with the application Archives live in a directory the server watches.
Adding, replacing or removing one takes effect without a rebuild or a restart. The server starts immediately Opening an archive reads only its metadata and table of contents.
The full-text index is built in the background, so documentation is readable
straight away and search becomes available shortly after. Archives describe themselves A generated nav.html carries the tree of pages and the bundle’s slug and
version together, so nothing is maintained twice.
Eclipse InfoCenter bundles are still supported, and still need no Eclipse or
OSGi machinery to serve. See Legacy Eclipse bundles . Any zip will do An archive needs a table of contents and some HTML.
It does not need to be an Eclipse help bundle, and it does not need to be
built by Maven. Markdown needs nothing installed Markdown is rendered inside the tool, so a directory of .md files becomes a
versioned, searchable manual with one command and no toolchain.
AsciiDoc and Typst are supported too, and need their own converters.

Quick start Run the server $ tobar-segais serve --content ./content The server listens on :8080 and serves whatever archives are in ./content .
It creates nothing: if the directory does not exist, the server exits rather
than silently serving an empty catalogue. Publish an archive Point the tool at a directory of documentation source.
Markdown needs nothing installed, so it is the shortest path from nothing to a
published manual: $ cat docs/nav.md
---
slug: handbook
version: 1.0.0
title: The Handbook
---

- [Introduction](index.md)

$ tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content
  detected markdown source
  converted 1 pages
content/handbook-1.0.0.zip (handbook 1.0.0, from nav, 1204 bytes) The catalogue picks it up within moments, without a restart.
Removing the file removes the documentation just as quickly. Or publish without a server Nothing above has to stay running. The same archives can be written out as a
static site and hosted anywhere that serves files: $ tobar-segais build --content ./content --out ./site
level=INFO msg="site generated" out=./site pages=1 assets=7 documents=1 The pages are rendered with the same templates the server uses, and search
still works — the index ships alongside them and is queried in the browser.
See Static sites . Check it worked $ curl -s localhost:8080/healthz
ok The server logs one line per archive as it loads, naming the slug, the version
and where the identity came from: level=INFO msg="loaded bundle" slug=handbook version=1.0.0 identity=metadata If a slug or version is not what you expected, that identity field tells you
which rule produced it. See Bundle format .

Bundle format A bundle is a .zip or .jar containing HTML pages and a navigation document. That is the whole format. In practice you will not write it by hand — tobar-segais bundle generates it from AsciiDoc, Markdown or Typst — but knowing the shape is useful when something does not appear where you expected. The navigation document nav.html at the archive root carries two things: the tree of pages, and the identity of the bundle. The tree is a nested list of links:
  • Introduction
  • Guides
    • Installing
Every href is relative to the archive root. An item with no link is a heading that groups its children without being a page itself. The order is the reading order: the previous and next links at the foot of each page follow it. Identity lives in the head, as meta elements — all of them optional: The Handbook Name Meaning tobar-segais.slug Used directly in the URL, so lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only. Defaults to the name part of the filename. tobar-segais.version Compared using semantic versioning, so 2.0.0 sorts above 1.16.0 and 2.0.0-rc1 sorts below 2.0.0 . Defaults to the version part of the filename. tobar-segais.title Optional. Shown in the catalogue and the sidebar. Defaults to the document title. tobar-segais.aliases Optional, comma separated. Additional slugs that resolve to this product, which is how a rename keeps old links working. An alias never displaces a real slug. tobar-segais.hidden Optional. true keeps the version reachable by direct link but leaves it out of the catalogue and out of latest . tobar-segais.priority Optional, a whole number, 0 by default. Orders the catalogue and the sidebar: higher comes first, and bundles sharing a priority are ordered by title. It may be negative, so an archive that should not be met first can sink itself without every other archive having to be raised above it. tobar-segais.copyright Optional. A notice about this documentation, shown in the footer of its pages. It overrides the server’s --copyright , so a bundle carrying its own notice keeps it wherever it is hosted. Elements may sit anywhere in the document; they are not required to be in the head. Typst, for one, emits them into the body. Nothing has to be declared A bundle need not say who it is. handbook-1.0.0.zip is handbook at 1.0.0 with no metadata at all: the version is taken from the end of the filename and the slug is what remains. An underscore works as well as a hyphen, and a v prefix on the version is accepted and dropped, so handbook_v1.0.0.zip reads the same way. Where no version can be found anywhere, the filename without its extension becomes the slug and the version is latest . So handbook.zip is served at /docs/handbook/latest/ . That is the right answer for a manual that simply has no versions, and it avoids an empty segment in every URL the bundle appears at. Sources are consulted in order — the navigation document, then an OSGi manifest, then Maven’s pom.properties , then the filename — and each fills only what is still missing. So a navigation document declaring a version but no slug keeps its version and takes the slug from the filename. That combination is the common one: the version is what a build knows, and the slug is usually what the filename already says. The load line in the log records where each part came from: level=INFO msg="loaded bundle" slug=handbook version=1.0.0 identity=nav+filename Everything else in the archive Images, stylesheets, PDFs and other files are served from wherever they sit in the archive. Relative links between pages work unchanged, so a documentation generator’s output can usually be zipped as-is. Pages are rendered inside the server’s own layout, which supplies the navigation, search and version picker. Only the body of each page is used, so whatever a generator puts in the head is discarded. Four things are removed from the body as it is rendered:

Source formats tobar-segais bundle detects the source language from the files in the
directory and runs the right converter.
Each format needs a navigation document and some pages.
Only AsciiDoc and Typst need a converter installed; Markdown is built in. Format Navigation Pages Converter asciidoc nav.adoc *.adoc asciidoctor or asciidoctor.js markdown nav.md *.md built in typst nav.typ *.typ typst html nav.html *.html none, copied as-is Each format has its own manual, written in that format and published the way
it describes: Bundles from AsciiDoc Bundles from Markdown Bundles from Typst Pointing at a converter Converters are looked up on PATH under their usual names.
Where that is not where yours lives — a user gem, a wrapper, a container — name it: $ tobar-segais bundle ./docs --tool ~/.gem/ruby/3.3.0/bin/asciidoctor
$ tobar-segais bundle ./docs --tool "bundle exec asciidoctor" The value may carry arguments, which are placed before the ones the tool
supplies. Quoting is honoured, so a path containing a space works. Both Asciidoctor implementations are supported and take the same flags.
Building this manual with asciidoctor.js instead of the Ruby implementation
produces byte-identical pages; only the generator string in the navigation
document differs. Partials A source file whose name begins with an underscore is a partial: pulled into
other pages, never a page itself.
Shared setup, a preamble, a chapter meant to be included — name it _common.typ or _preamble.adoc and it stays out of the navigation and out
of the bundle. This matters most for Typst, whose native model joins files with #include into a single document. Typst offers a second route: its bundle export lets one compilation write
several files, each declared with #document("page.html")[…​] .
Name that source book.typ or main.typ and omit nav.typ , and the tool
uses bundle export, so a book can stay one source and still publish as a
multi-page bundle.
See Books and multiple files . Pass --format to override detection.
HTML is only detected when no other source is present, so a directory holding
both sources and a previous build is still recognised by its sources. Why the converters are invoked this way Converters are invoked as plainly as they allow.
Rather than a flag per tool to suppress each thing a bundle does not want, the
output is cleaned afterwards: stylesheets and generator footers are removed,
from output this tool generated and from output it did not. That is why AsciiDoc is simply: $ asciidoctor -o page.html page.adoc Asciidoctor embeds around 29 KB of CSS in every full document and a footer
carrying a "Last updated" timestamp, which would otherwise change every page
on every build. Both are removed. The document title stays, because in full
output it is already an <h1> in the header. The navigation document keeps one flag, -a docinfosubs=attributes , because
that is what substitutes the slug and version into its head. It is converted
as a whole document for the same reason: its head is the point. Heading levels Generators disagree about what the top level means: Asciidoctor and goldmark
make a document title an h1 , Typst reserves h1 for itself and starts
content at h2 , and DocBook XSL emits a chapter title as h2 . The server shifts headings so the shallowest one on a page is an h1 .
A page therefore reads the same whatever produced it, and no format has to
compensate — which matters because Typst cannot. Markdown Markdown needs nothing installed: it is rendered in-process with goldmark , the renderer Hugo uses.
The dialect is GitHub Flavored Markdown — CommonMark plus tables,
strikethrough, task lists and autolinks — with definition lists and footnotes
enabled as well. Identity goes in YAML front matter on the navigation document: ---
slug: handbook
version: 1.0.0
title: The Handbook
---

- [Introduction](index.md)
- Guides
  - [Installing](install.md) Links point at the .md sources and are rewritten to the generated pages.
Because the rewriting happens on the parsed document rather than by editing
text, reference-style links and links split across lines are handled
correctly, and anything with a scheme is left alone. Typst #html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.slug", content: "handbook"))
#html.elem("meta", attrs: (name: "tobar-segais.version", content: "1.0.0"))
#html.elem("title")[The Handbook]

- #link("index.html")[Introduction]
- Guides
  - #link("install.html")[Installing] Note Typst’s HTML export is marked experimental by its authors and must be enabled
with --features html , which the tool does for you.
Treat it as a preview rather than a promise. Its exporter also shifts headings down a level, so = becomes <h2> .
Nothing needs doing about that: the server normalises heading levels when it
renders a page, so the shallowest heading becomes h1 whatever produced it. Plain HTML If a generator already produces HTML, name its navigation document nav.html and pack the directory as-is.
Anything the tool does not recognise as source — images, stylesheets, PDFs — is copied into the bundle with its layout intact.

Versions Every archive declares a version.
Archives sharing a slug are grouped into one product, and the version picker in
the toolbar moves between them. Ordering Versions are ordered by semantic versioning precedence.
Versions that are not strict semver are accepted where the intent is clear: 1.16 is read as 1.16.0 . A pre-release sorts below the release it precedes, so 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT is older
than 2.0.0 and will not be chosen as the latest version. A version that cannot be parsed at all sorts last and is never selected as the
latest.
It remains reachable at its own URL. An archive that declares no version at all is served as latest , which is
both its version and the alias every product answers to.
Mixing an unversioned archive with versioned ones under the same slug is
therefore possible but confusing, and the unversioned one will sort last. URLs Each version has a stable address: /docs/handbook/1.0.0/guides/install.html latest resolves to the newest visible version: /docs/handbook/latest/guides/install.html Requesting the product on its own redirects to the latest version: /docs/handbook/  ->  /docs/handbook/2.0.0/ Switching version keeps your position in the document, so the picker moves you
to the same page in the other version.
If that page does not exist there, you get the not-found page rather than a
silent redirect to somewhere else. Retiring a version Set hidden = true in its metadata.
The version disappears from the catalogue and from latest , but existing links
to it keep working.
Removing the archive from the directory removes it entirely.

Configuration The server is started with tobar-segais serve and configured by flags. Flag Default Meaning --content ./content Directory of .zip and .jar archives to serve. --addr :8080 Address to listen on. --poll 30s How often to rescan the content directory. --default (none) Slug to serve at / instead of the catalogue index. --copyright (none) Notice about the documentation itself, shown in the footer. --debug false Verbose logging, including a line per request. Serving one product A server hosting a single product does not need a catalogue listing one item.
Name it with --default and / redirects to its latest version: $ tobar-segais serve --content ./content --default handbook The catalogue stays available at every other address, and the version picker
still works. If the slug does not resolve — misspelled, or its archive has not loaded — the catalogue is served instead and a warning is logged once.
The root never fails because of a typo in a flag. Watching the content directory The server watches the content directory for changes and reloads what has
changed.
Where the platform supports filesystem notifications it uses them; where it
does not — which in practice means some network filesystems and container
volume drivers — it falls back to polling at the --poll interval. Polling also runs as a backstop even when notifications are working, because a
dropped event would otherwise leave the catalogue silently stale. Writes are allowed to settle before an archive is read, so copying a large file
into the directory does not cause it to be read half-written. Reloading Only archives that have actually changed are reopened.
An archive that has not moved is left alone, so a reload costs one directory
listing. Removing a file closes its archive and drops it from the catalogue. Saying who owns the documentation The footer carries a notice for Tobar Segais itself — it is Apache-licensed,
and that does not change. What it cannot know is who owns the manuals being
served, so nothing is claimed about them unless you say so: $ tobar-segais serve --content ./content \
    --copyright "Copyright © 2026 Example Ltd. All rights reserved." The text is shown above the software’s own notice, on every page that does not
say otherwise. A bundle can say otherwise. tobar-segais.copyright in its navigation
document overrides this flag for that bundle’s pages, which is the better
place for it: the notice is about the documentation, so it belongs to the
documentation and travels with it wherever the archive is served. Use the flag
for what is true of the whole site, and the metadata for what is true of one
manual. A server hosting several owners' documentation should set no flag at
all and let each archive speak for itself. See Bundle format .

Search Search covers the text of every page listed in every table of contents, across
all versions of all products. Indexing happens in the background The server does not wait for the index before it starts serving.
Opening an archive reads its metadata and table of contents only, which is a
few kilobytes; the index is built afterwards, on a background worker. Until it is ready the search page says so, and reports its progress, rather
than returning an empty result set that looks like an answer. When archives are added or removed the index is rebuilt and replaced in one
step, so a search never sees a half-built index. How queries are matched All terms must appear A query of stylesheet customization returns only pages containing both.
Documentation search is a lookup rather than a discovery engine, and partial
matches mostly produce noise. Titles count for more A term in a page title weighs more heavily than the same term in the body. Results are ranked Ranking uses term frequency against how common the term is across the corpus,
so a word that appears everywhere contributes little. Filtering Restrict a search to one product or one version with query parameters: /search?q=install&slug=handbook
/search?q=install&slug=handbook&version=1.0.0 Searching from within a product carries the product filter automatically.

Static sites The same content can be published without running anything. tobar-segais build renders every page to a file and writes them, with the
search index and the assets, into an output directory: $ tobar-segais build --content ./content --out ./site
level=INFO msg="site generated" out=./site pages=42 assets=7 documents=42 The result is plain files. Upload them to GitHub Pages, an S3 bucket, or any
web server, and there is nothing left to run or keep alive. What you get, and what you lose Pages are rendered with the same templates the server uses, so a generated
site looks and behaves like a served one. Navigation, the version picker and
the table of contents are all there, and search still works: the index is
written alongside the pages as search-index.json and queried in the browser. What a static site cannot do is notice a new archive. A served catalogue picks
up a change to the content directory within moments; a generated one is a
snapshot, and publishing a new version means running build again. That is
the trade, and for documentation that changes when a release is cut it is
usually the right one — the build already exists, and it can write the site. Options Flag Default Meaning --content ./content Directory of .zip and .jar archives to publish. --out , -o ./site Directory to write the generated site into. --site (none) Path the site is rooted at, if it is not the root of the domain. --default (none) Slug to publish at / instead of the catalogue index. --copyright (none) Notice about the documentation itself, shown in the footer. A bundle
declaring tobar-segais.copyright overrides it for its own pages. --debug false Verbose logging. publish is accepted as an alias for build . A generated page says it was published by Tobar Segais where a served one says
it was served by it. The difference is worth having: a served page is as
current as the content directory, and a published one is as current as the
last build. Sites below the root of a domain A GitHub Pages project site is served from https://user.github.io/repo/ ,
not from the root. Every absolute link the site writes has to carry that
prefix, so give it: $ tobar-segais build --content ./content --out ./site --site /repo Get this wrong and the pages render but the stylesheet, the search index and
every link between pages point one directory too high. Serving the output
locally is the quickest way to be sure — but serve it from the same depth it
will be published at, or the mistake will not show. In a release pipeline The two commands compose: build the bundles from source, then build the site
from the bundles. $ tobar-segais bundle ./docs --out ./content
$ tobar-segais build --content ./content --out ./site --site /handbook Keeping the archives — rather than generating the site straight from source — is what makes the version picker work. build publishes every archive it
finds, so a content directory holding handbook-1.0.0.zip and handbook-1.1.0.zip produces a site with both versions and a picker that
moves between them. Add each release to the directory and keep it there.

Legacy Eclipse bundles Tobar Segais began as a container for Eclipse InfoCenter help bundles, and
still serves them without any Eclipse or OSGi machinery.
Nothing needs to be repackaged. These formats are supported for archives that already exist.
New documentation should use the bundle format , which is
generated for you. Identity Where an archive has no navigation document of its own, the slug and version
are resolved from the first of these that answers: nav.html — the convention, described in Bundle format . OSGi manifest headers Bundle-SymbolicName and Bundle-Version . Maven’s META-INF/maven/**/pom.properties . The filename, read as name-version . The filename alone, with no version. The server logs which rule produced the answer, as identity= on the load
line, so an unexpected slug can be traced without guesswork. Note plugin.xml carries an id and a version , and both are deliberately
ignored.
In bundles generated from the DocBook sample they are almost always left as com.example.help and 1.0 , which would collide across every product and
report every version as the same. Table of contents Where there is no nav.html , the server reads a legacy Eclipse plugin.xml and follows its org.eclipse.help.toc extension, preferring the entry marked primary . Failing that, it looks for a toc.xml at the archive root. toc.xml and nav.html describe the same tree in different notation; the
format is chosen by file extension. Generator navigation Documentation generators often bake their own navigation into each page.
DocBook XSL, for instance, emits Prev/Next tables at the top and bottom of
every page. The server removes those, because it provides the same navigation itself from
the table of contents.
Reading order comes from the table of contents rather than from whatever the
generator recorded, so it stays correct if the bundle is reorganised. Correcting an old bundle An Eclipse bundle names itself through its OSGi manifest, which was written
when the bundle was built and cannot be changed now without rebuilding it. If
the slug, version or title that comes out is not what you want, put a .toml file beside the archive and say so there instead. See Bundle format .

Chapter 2. Building Prev Next Chapter 2. Building By default the Tobar Segais web application does not bundle any documentation, so in order to have a useful
      web application you must build a custom version that includes the desired InfoCenter plugin bundles. The easiest way to build the Tobar Segais web application is using Apache Maven's WAR Overlays feature.
      Start by creating a basic pom.xml that depends on the Tobar Segais Web application: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
      http://maven.apache.org/maven-v4_0_0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.mydomain.reversed</groupId>
  <artifactId>docs-webapp</artifactId>
  <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>war</packaging>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.tobarsegais</groupId>
      <artifactId>tobar-segais-webapp</artifactId>
      <version>1.16</version>
      <type>war</type>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.mydomain.reversed</groupId>
      <artifactId>docs-infocenter-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
      <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>
        <executions>
          <execution>
            <phase>generate-resources</phase>
            <goals>
              <goal>copy-dependencies</goal>
            </goals>
            <configuration>
              <outputDirectory>
                ${project.build.directory}/${project.build.finalName}/WEB-INF/bundles
              </outputDirectory>
              <includeScope>provided</includeScope>
            </configuration>
          </execution>
        </executions>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>

</project> To build the web application, just invoke Apache Maven with a phase of “package” or later, e.g. mvn package The generated .war file can then be deployed in any Servlet container that supports the Servlet 2.5
      specification. Prev Next Chapter 1. Introduction Home Chapter 3. Customization

Chapter 3. Customization Prev Next Chapter 3. Customization Table of Contents Introduction Stylesheet customization Navbar customization Icon customization Introduction Not everyone will be happy with everything about how the Tobar Segais web application looks.
        However, you will be happy to know that the Tobar Segais web application supports a number of customization
        points to enable you to get it looking just the way you want. Prev Next Chapter 2. Building Home Stylesheet customization

Stylesheet customization Prev Chapter 3. Customization Next Stylesheet customization The core look of Tobar Segais is based on Twitter Bootstrap. Any custom full build of Bootstrap 2.0.x should
        work as a drop in replacement that offers the customized look and feel. Assuming you are building your Tobar Segais web application using the technique described in Chapter 2 all you need do is create the file src/main/webapp/css/bootstrap.min.css containing the minified version of your custom build
        of Twitter Bootstrap. If you have customized versions of the Glyph Icons, these should be put at the paths src/main/webapp/img/glyphicons-halflings.png and src/main/webapp/img/glyphicons-halflings-white.png If you just want to apply some simple tweaks to the CSS after Twitter Bootstrap is loaded
        all you need to do is create the file src/main/webapp/css/custom.css this file is included after all the other CSS files have been included. Prev Up Next Chapter 3. Customization Home Navbar customization

Navbar customization Prev Chapter 3. Customization Next Navbar customization The Navbar at the top of the page can be easily customized by providing a replacement JSP Fragment. Assuming you are building your Tobar Segais web application using the technique described in Chapter 2 all you need do is create the file src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/custom-navbar.jspf containing the custom navbar. For example, the default Navbar has the following custom-navbar.jspf : <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" language="java" %>
